title: Romance novel
wiki_lead:
Romance, or romance fiction, is the genre of narrative fiction whose works focus on the budding emotional, sexual, and loving relationship between two or more characters, often concluding with an emotionally satisfying or optimistic ending. Traditionally its most common format is the romance novel. 
Romance novels encompass numerous subgenres. While women have traditionally been considered the primary readers of romance novels, a 2017 study commissioned by the Romance Writers of America found that men accounted for 18% of romance book buyers
The genre of works retroactively referred to as "romance novels" existed as far back as Greece in the Roman era. Precursors can also be found in the literary fiction of the 18th and 19th centuries, including Samuel Richardson's sentimental novel Pamela, or Virtue Rewarded (1740) and the novels of Jane Austen. Austen inspired Georgette Heyer, the British author of historical romance set around Austen's lifetime, as well as detective fiction. Heyer's first romance novel, The Black Moth (1921), was set in 1751.
The British Publisher, Mills & Boon, shifted focus towards romance fiction during the 1930s. Beginning in 1957, its novels were distributed in North America by Harlequin Enterprises, which expanded reader access through their direct marketing and mass market retail distribution.
An early American example of a mass-market romance was Kathleen E. Woodiwiss' The Flame and the Flower (1972), published by Avon Books. This was the first single-title romance novel to be published as an original paperback in the US. In the United Kingdom, Georgette Heyer's novels played a significant role in the development of historical romance. Some later editions have been revised to remove or alter certain stereotypes.
Strong sales of popular romance novels have contributed to the genre becoming one of the largest segments of the global book market. Although romance fiction was popular beforehand, the market experienced significant growth during the 1970s, with the addition of more subcategories and an increased number of single-title romances, but authors started pushing the boundaries of genre and plot, as well as creating more contemporary characters.

Definition
Women will pick up a romance novel knowing what to expect, and this foreknowledge of the reader is very important. When the hero and heroine meet and fall in love, maybe they don't know they're in love but the reader does. Then a conflict will draw them apart, but you know in the end they'll be back together, and preferably married or planning to be by page 192.
According to the Romance Writers of America, the main plot of a mass-market romance novel must revolve about the two people as they develop romantic love for each other and work to build a relationship. Both the conflict and the climax of the novel should be directly related to that core theme of developing a romantic relationship, although the novel can also contain subplots that do not specifically relate to the main characters' romantic love. Furthermore, a romance novel must have an "emotionally satisfying and optimistic ending."
Leslie Gelbman, a president of Berkley Books, defines the genre as stating that romance must make the "romantic relationship between the hero and the heroine ... the core of the book." In general, romance novels reward characters who are good people and penalize those who are evil, and a couple who fights for and believes in their relationship will likely be rewarded with unconditional love. Bestselling author Nora Roberts states the romance genre in books "are about the celebration of falling in love and emotion and commitment, and all of those things we really want."

grok_lead: The romance novel is a genre of popular fiction that primarily focuses on the romantic relationship and love between two protagonists, typically resolving with a happy ending that affirms the centrality of this bond. Emerging in its modern form from 18th-century works like Samuel Richardson's Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded, which emphasized courtship and moral virtue in romantic narratives, the genre evolved through 19th-century novels by authors such as Jane Austen and the BrontÃ« sisters, blending social observation with emotional intimacy. The mass-market romance novel took shape in the 20th century with publishers like Mills & Boon and Harlequin, standardizing short, formulaic stories of heterosexual attraction and resolution that catered to female readers seeking escapism amid domestic realities. By the late 20th and early 21st centuries, romance diversified into subgenres including historical, contemporary, paranormal, and erotical variants, while maintaining core elements of conflict-driven pursuit of love and emotional fulfillment. Economically dominant, the genre generated over $1.44 billion in U.S. revenue in 2023, with print unit sales reaching 39 million copies, outpacing other fiction categories and demonstrating sustained consumer demand despite scholarly critiques of its repetitive structures and reinforcement of traditional relational dynamics. Predominantly authored and read by women (82% of readers), making it the most popular fiction genre among female audiences and accounting for 18% of adult fiction sales, romance novels have faced dismissal from literary establishments as formulaic or ideologically conservative, yet their commercial success underscores a causal appeal rooted in the empirical universality of romantic aspirations and narrative closure.
